title: Drift monitoring at portfolio scale: per-test thresholds versus family-wise and false-discovery-rate control

primary_hypothesis.statement: In a simulated portfolio of N=1000 models with F=20 monitored features each (daily windows of n=200 rows, reference samples of m=1000 rows, two-sample KS tests), applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at q=0.05 to each day's family of tests reduces the mean number of false feature-level alarms per day by at least 90% relative to per-test thresholds at alpha=0.05, while detecting within 3 days at least 80% of the simulated drift events that per-test thresholds detect within 3 days.
primary_endpoint: R_FA = 1 - FA_BH / FA_per-test, where FA = mean number of rejected tests per day whose feature is not drifted on that day
RR = recall3_BH / recall3_per-test, where recall3 = fraction of drift events with at least one drifted feature rejected within 3 days of onset
primary_hypothesis.unit_of_replication: simulation seed (5 seeds: 0,1,2,3,4); endpoints are computed per seed, then mean and t-based 95% CI across seeds
primary_hypothesis.baseline: per-test thresholds at alpha=0.05 (no multiplicity control), which is how single-model drift monitors are typically configured
comparators: Bonferroni at family-wise alpha=0.05 per day
hierarchical: per-model Bonferroni-combined p-value, then BH across models at q=0.05
primary_hypothesis.decision_rule: SUPPORTED if the lower 95% CI bound of R_FA >= 0.90 AND the lower 95% CI bound of RR >= 0.80. REFUTED if the upper 95% CI bound of R_FA < 0.90 OR the upper 95% CI bound of RR < 0.80. Otherwise INCONCLUSIVE.
primary_hypothesis.falsification_rule: H1 is falsified if BH retains less than 80% of per-test 3-day event recall with the whole 95% CI below 0.80, or if it removes less than 90% of false alarms with the whole 95% CI below 0.90.

secondary_hypotheses.statement: The PSI rule-of-thumb threshold 0.1 (B=10 reference-quantile bins, 0.5 additive smoothing) is not sample-size invariant: on no-drift windows drawn from real public tabular features, its false alarm rate at window size n=100 exceeds its false alarm rate at n=2000 by more than 10 percentage points.
secondary_hypotheses.endpoint: difference in no-drift false alarm rate (numeric features, averaged over features), per seed
secondary_hypotheses.decision_rule: SUPPORTED if the lower 95% CI bound of the difference > 0.10; REFUTED if the upper bound < 0.10; else INCONCLUSIVE.

secondary_hypotheses.statement: On the electricity (Elec2) stream with its real temporal order, weekly input-drift alarms (KS per feature with BH at q=0.05 across features) and weekly performance-drop alarms (one-sided two-proportion z-test of batch error versus validation error at alpha=0.05) agree at most fairly: Cohen's kappa < 0.4.
secondary_hypotheses.endpoint: Cohen's kappa between the two weekly alarm series over 40 monitored weeks, per run (5 runs with different training windows and model seeds)
secondary_hypotheses.decision_rule: SUPPORTED if the upper 95% CI bound of kappa < 0.4; REFUTED if the lower bound >= 0.4; else INCONCLUSIVE.

exploratory: TPR at a calibrated per-window FPR of 0.05 for PSI, KL, Wasserstein-1, KS, and binned chi-square across injected drift types, magnitudes, and window sizes on real feature distributions (adult, bank-marketing, electricity)
detection delay under a gradual mean-shift ramp in a streaming setting
portfolio breakpoints: within-model feature correlation (rho=0.6), 10% missing test results, window size 100 and 500
simulation_disclosure: All drift in the detector benchmark and the portfolio study is injected (simulated). Only H3 uses a real temporal shift.
